identity.name: Danelaw
alt_names: Kingdom of York (as its last remnant)

land.text: East Anglia, the East Midlands and Yorkshire, as Cliopatria's Danelaw shape of 878

predecessors.note: Danelaw page: 'The Danelaw approximately covered Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands, and the East of England.' The Viking settlements dossier has the matching loss in 878.

land.text: the eastern Midlands that Cliopatria adds in 880

predecessors.note: The Mercia dossier records the Danish seizure of the eastern half of Mercia at 877; this dossier has it at 880, the year the shape grows.

land.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

successors.note: Danelaw page: 'Viking rule ended when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out of Northumbria in 954.' The Northumbria page has Eadred appoint Oswulf earl of the whole of Northumbria. Cliopatria's Danelaw row runs to 959; the pages end Viking rule in 954.

capitals.name: York (Jorvik)
capitals.note: No opened page names a capital of the Danelaw, which was a region of Danish law with several Danish kings (Guthrum in East Anglia, the Five Boroughs' armies, Halfdan and his heirs in Yorkshire). York is where the Viking kings of the north reigned (Kingdom of York page: Ragnall 'king at York', Eric 'king in York') and it is the only city of the 922 remnant.

keyframe_review.note: 45,807 km2 in shapes.csv (about 49.6 thousand by cell count): East Anglia (57 cells), the East Midlands and Yorkshire up to the Tees. Danelaw page: 'The Danelaw approximately covered Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands, and the East of England'; 'The Danes now controlled East Anglia, Northumbria and Mercia'. The page gives no area figure. Wedmore and Edington are 878; the treaty line is dated only 'between 878 and Guthrum's death in 890'.

55,257 km2: +43 cells (10.9 thousand km2, 1.6 W-0.1 W, 51.6-53.3 N) of the Midlands. The Danelaw page names no change at 880 and calls the Five Boroughs (Leicester, Nottingham, Derby, Stamford, Lincoln) the Danes' strongholds. Confidence 1 in the ledger. unverified: page budget.

54,513 km2: four cells of the lower Thames and Essex (1.0 thousand km2) leave: Treaty page, 'some historians have suggested that the treaty would not have been finalised until Alfred reoccupied the city in 886', which 'ascribes Viking-held London to Alfred'. Boundary in the treaty: 'up the Thames, and then up [the Lea], and along the Lea to its source', then 'in a straight line to [Bedford]', then 'up [the Ouse] to [Watling Street]'.

correction.text: valid for 911-914 only; from 915 the reconquest removes Bedford, then Northampton, Cambridge, East Anglia and Derby (917), then the rest of the south (918)

keyframe_review.note: 54,579 km2, unchanged to 921, but Edward's and Æthelflæd's reconquest cuts it away from 914/915: Thurketil of Bedford submits (late 914), Edward 'occupied Bedford' (915), Northampton, Cambridge and East Anglia submit (917), Derby falls to Æthelflæd (917), Leicester (early 918), Stamford and Nottingham (918); 'All the people who had settled in Mercia, both Danish and English, submitted to him' (Chronicle 918). Cliopatria keeps the whole shape to 921 and drops it in 922, four years late. The shape stands for 911-914 only; see the new keyframes 915, 917 and 918. [orchestrator 2 Nov 2026: from/to set to 911..914 from this entry's own 'valid for 911-914 only'; without them the compiler drew the shape for all its Cliopatria years, overlapping the next keyframe (window p1100-p1199 report)]

correction.text: the Danelaw without Bedford, occupied by Edward in 915

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 915-916: the 911 shape without Bedford. 'The following year Edward occupied Bedford' and built a fort on the south bank of the Great Ouse (915); 916: Edward returned to Essex and built a fort at Maldon, and helped Thurketil and his followers leave England.

correction.text: the Danelaw without Bedford, Northampton, Cambridge, East Anglia and Derby

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 917: after Tempsford (late summer 917: the last Danish king of East Anglia was killed) the Danes of Northampton submitted to Edward and the armies of Cambridge and East Anglia also submitted; Æthelflæd captured Derby. At the end of 917 only the Danish armies of Leicester, Stamford, Nottingham and Lincoln were still holding out besides York. Colchester was taken but not held.

correction.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 918-921: the York remnant only. Leicester submits to Æthelflæd without a fight and Stamford and Nottingham to Edward (early to mid 918); 'All the people who had settled in Mercia, both Danish and English, submitted to him.' Lincoln is unclear ('It is unclear whether Lincoln submitted. Coins of Viking York in the early 920s were probably minted there'); Cliopatria's 922 shape has no Lincolnshire cells. The Danes of York offered Æthelflæd their allegiance in early 918; 'the Norse Vikings took York in 919'.

Æthelstan page: 'he conquered the last remaining Viking kingdom, York' in 927; the shape then belongs to England until 939 (see the new keyframes 927 and 939). keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 927-938: the Danelaw has no land. Æthelstan page (927): 'he conquered the last remaining Viking kingdom, York', making him 'the first Anglo-Saxon ruler of the whole of England'; York stays English until Æthelstan dies on 27 October 939. Cliopatria draws the Danelaw shape through these years; the England dossier holds York (gain 927).

keyframe_review.note: 16,474 km2: the shape belongs to 939-943 only (new keyframe 939). 936-938 York is Æthelstan's; 944-946 Eadmund holds it ('Edmund was able to expel the Viking leaders from Northumbria', annals of 944).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe 939-943: York under Olaf Guthfrithson. 'After Æthelstan's death, the men of York immediately chose' him (Æthelstan page); Olaf 'took over Northumbria with minimal opposition' and in 941 'invaded Mercia and East Anglia' (York page). The page does not map the extent of his Northumbria beyond the York remnant.

correction.text: the York remnant, contested 947-954; none after 954

keyframe_review.note: 16,603 km2: York contested between Eric Bloodaxe and Eadred from 947 to 954. York page: Eric established himself as king in York and Eadred raided Northumbria and drove him out (947-948); Olaf Cuaran restored 950-952; 'In 952 Eric removed him and then reigned in Northumbria till 954', killed at Stainmore. Valid for 947-954; Cliopatria runs the row to 959, five years past the end of Viking rule.

region.text: Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands and the East of England

ledger.note: 878: after Edington the Danes hold East Anglia, the East Midlands and Yorkshire: the Danelaw. 'The Danes now controlled East Anglia, Northumbria and Mercia, with only Wessex continuing to resist'; Alfred defeats Guthrum at Edington in 878 and the Treaty of Wedmore follows. The treaty line is dated 'between 878 and Guthrum's death in 890' (Treaty page), so 878 is Cliopatria's start, not a page's founding date.

region.text: the eastern Midlands, the later Five Boroughs

ledger.note: 880: Cliopatria's Danelaw grows by 43 cells of the Midlands (10.9 thousand km2, 1.6-0.1 W, 51.6-53.3 N). The Danelaw page names no change at this date: page silent. The Mercia dossier records the Danish seizure of the eastern half of Mercia at 877.

region.text: London and the lower Thames cells held by the Danes

ledger.note: 886: Alfred holds London. 'Some historians have suggested that the treaty would not have been finalised until Alfred reoccupied the city in 886'; the treaty 'ascribes Viking-held London to Alfred' and fixes the boundary up the Thames and the Lea, to Bedford, up the Ouse to Watling Street. The treaty's own date is 'between 878 and Guthrum's death in 890'.

region.text: the Danish lands south of the Humber: East Anglia, the East Midlands, Essex and Lincolnshire

ledger.note: 915: Edward's reconquest of the Danelaw begins in earnest. The Danelaw page: Edward 'conquered Danish territories in the Midlands and East Anglia in a series of campaigns in the 910s'; first ground taken is Bedford ('The following year Edward occupied Bedford', after Thurketil's submission in late 914).
915: Edward occupies Bedford and builds a fort on the south bank of the Great Ouse.

917: the Danes of Northampton, Cambridge and East Anglia submit to Edward. Late summer 917: the English stormed Tempsford and killed the last Danish king of East Anglia; Colchester was taken but not held.
917: Æthelflæd, Lady of the Mercians, takes Derby ('Æthelflæd captured Derby'; Danelaw page: 'took the borough of Derby').
early 918: Leicester submits to Æthelflæd 'without a fight' (Danelaw page: 'The borough of Leicester submitted peaceably to Æthelflæd's rule').

minus.text: the Danish lands south of the Humber: East Anglia, the East Midlands, Essex and Lincolnshire

region.text: Stamford, Nottingham, Lincoln and the remaining Danish shires

ledger.note: 918: Stamford surrenders to Edward and Nottingham follows; the Chronicle for 918 states 'All the people who had settled in Mercia, both Danish and English, submitted to him.' Lincoln is unclear on the page; the remaining Danish shires south of the Humber are Cliopatria's reading.

region.text: the Danish lands south of the Humber: East Anglia, the East Midlands, Essex and Lincolnshire

ledger.note: 918: the Danelaw south of the Humber is Edward's. The Danes of York alone remain outside; they offered Æthelflæd their allegiance before she died on 12 June 918.

919: the Hiberno-Norse take York. Edward page: 'The Norse Vikings took York in 919'; Ragnall is king of York in 920 (Bakewell, 'chose him as father and lord', a submission historians such as Davidson doubt). The York page: the Battle of Corbridge 'did allow Ragnall to establish himself as king at York'; Sihtric replaces him in 921. Same state and colour; the Danish dynasty gives way to the Uí Ímair line.

region.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

ledger.note: 927: Æthelstan conquers York. 'He conquered the last remaining Viking kingdom, York', the Danelaw's last land; the page gives no month (the England dossier places it with the Eamont meeting of 12 July 927).

939: York takes Olaf Guthfrithson as king. 'After Æthelstan's death, the men of York immediately chose the Viking king of Dublin, Olaf Guthfrithson, as their king' (Æthelstan page; died 27 October 939); the York page: he 'took over Northumbria with minimal opposition'.

region.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

ledger.note: 944: Eadmund drives the Vikings out. 'The annals for 944 agree that Edmund was able to expel the Viking leaders from Northumbria.'

region.text: York and the land round it, contested between the Viking kings and Eadred

ledger.note: 947: Eric Bloodaxe takes York and the contest with Eadred begins. Eric established himself as king in York and Eadred's response was to raid Northumbria and drive him out; Olaf Cuaran was restored 950 to 952, and Eric again 952-954. The England dossier's contest runs 947-954.

region.text: York and the land round it

ledger.note: 954: Eric is killed at Stainmore and the contest ends. Eadred's forces killed Eric at the Battle of Stainmore, which ended Scandinavian rule, and the earls who followed were appointed by the kings of England (York page).

region.text: York and the land round it

ledger.note: 954: Viking rule ends. Danelaw page: 'Viking rule ended when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out of Northumbria in 954'; the Northumbria infobox: 'Last Viking king expelled by King Eadred: 954'. York becomes part of the English earldom of Northumbria.

region.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

ledger.note: 954: the Danelaw ends as a state. The page never dates an end of the Danelaw itself ('The Danelaw appeared in legislation as late as the early 12th century'); the end of Viking rule in the north in 954 is the last page-dated event. Cliopatria's row runs to 959.

wars.name: Battle of Edington
wars.outcome: Alfred defeats Guthrum at Edington; the Treaty of Wedmore follows and the Danes keep East Anglia and the north.
wars.note: The Danelaw page also names the capture of Wareham (876) as the Danes breaking the peace.

wars.name: Battle of Tettenhall
wars.outcome: A Mercian and West Saxon force dealt a 'decisive defeat' to an invading Northumbrian army; the Viking kings Eowils and Halfdan II were killed 'at Tettenhall on 5 August 910' (York page).
wars.note: The Danelaw page's timeline puts Tettenhall at 911; the Edward and York pages say 910.

wars.name: Edward the Elder's and Æthelflæd's reconquest of the Danelaw

wars.outcome: By the end of 918 the Danes of Bedford, Northampton, Cambridge, East Anglia, Derby, Leicester, Stamford and Nottingham had submitted; only York stayed Danish (Norse from 919).
wars.note: Fall of the Five Boroughs: Derby 917, Leicester 918, Stamford and Nottingham 918; Lincoln unclear.

wars.outcome: Æthelstan 'conquered the last remaining Viking kingdom, York' in 927.
wars.note: William of Malmesbury's account on the York page: Gofraid at Dacre, besieged York, was captured by Æthelstan.

zones.text: the York remnant: Yorkshire between the Humber and the Tees

wars.outcome: York chooses Olaf Guthfrithson in 939; he invades Mercia and East Anglia in 941; Eadmund expels the Viking leaders from Northumbria in 944.

wars.name: Eric Bloodaxe and Eadred

zones.text: York and Northumbria north of the Humber

wars.outcome: Eric rules at York in 947, is driven out in 948, rules again 952-954 and is killed at Stainmore; Eadred then holds Northumbria.

certainty.note: No boundary is dated; the treaty line is placed only 'between 878 and Guthrum's death in 890'.

The treaty of Alfred and Guthrum fixes the frontier up the Thames and the Lea to Bedford and up the Ouse to Watling Street; the date of the line is uncertain (878-890). The northern frontier with Bernicia and the Tees line are soft throughout.
The frontier moves with each fortress taken (915-918) and the York remnant has no dated boundary beyond the Tees and the Humber.

notes: Five pages were budgeted and used. Cliopatria's Danelaw row (878-959) is one region of Danish law that Edward and Æthelflæd reduced to the York remnant in 918, yet its shapes keep the whole until 921 and the remnant until 959; the corrections above (new keyframes 915, 917, 918, 927, 939, 944) override Cliopatria's shapes in the years they cover, and the Danelaw has no land at all in 927-938 and 944-946 (York is English). Disagreements between pages: Tettenhall 910 (Edward and York pages) vs 911 (Danelaw timeline); the Danelaw page puts the treaty at 886-890, the Treaty page between 878 and 890. The England dossier holds York continuously from 927 to its contest_start of 947 and has no 939-944 interlude of Olaf Guthfrithson; a gap-filler should add it there (events 939 and 944 in this dossier). The Danelaw dossier ends in 954, not Cliopatria's 959; the Danelaw as a region of law outlasted this by two centuries (Danelaw page, 'as late as the early 12th century') but is not drawn. Capital: York is a convention (see the capitals note); no opened page names a Danelaw capital. Counterparts needing dossiers: the Five Boroughs' armies and Guthrum's East Anglia have none (the East Anglia dossier ends in 869); the Hiberno-Norse kings of York have no separate dossier. Region names the gazetteer lacks: none (admin-1 units only). Quotation marks enclose strings the page-fetch tool returned as quotations; other wording paraphrases its summary of the page, which was read by WebFetch only (no raw page text). The two validator warnings 'resolves to no cells' are the deliberately empty corrections of the new keyframes 927 and 944.
